**The monitor is up and proven.** `tools/ask_monitor.py`, armed persistently against the mini, watching for `asked`/`proposed`. Currently quiet — no real asks standing.

Two bugs found and fixed by actually testing it rather than trusting it:

1. **A world appearing after arming was swallowed silently.** I seeded a new log's history into the seen-set without reporting it — which is exactly the first-time-asker case, the one that matters most. Now a log that appears mid-run is arrivals, not history.
2. **Tailing an open handle went permanently silent after the first write.** `remember` writes each log by temp-file-and-rename, so the handle kept reading the replaced inode; compaction rewrites from the top too. Replaced with a stat-and-reread sweep — the log is bounded at 512 compacted records, so the honest read is also the cheap one, and the seen-set keeps re-reads quiet.

Proof, in order: backlog of three shipped asks read correctly from history → a probe ask filed into a tooling world appeared as `BACKLOG` on restart → a third probe fired while watching arrived as a live `ASK` within the poll beat, carrying status, `t`, tool and birthplace path. Probe world cleared and removed; the mini's state dir is back to its three real worlds. Committed as build-in-waiting.

The line it prints is the triage brief's raw material: `t` is the `asks#<t>` anchor, `at` is the proposed parent node, and the proposal is the contract paragraph.

One note on what the monitor cannot see: `stamp_ask.py` writes through `POST /diag/context`, which is now `same-door` — so my own `building` stamps will show up in this stream too if I ever run it with `--all-statuses`. With the default filter they don't, which is what you want.

### p7
*2026-08-23 10:06*

> great, nice work! could you briefly explain to me 1) the workflow for handling user "asks" from miso, and 2) how this workflow is expressed within claude code?

**1) What happens to an ask**

You type a wish into the ask box on your phone.

- Miso first tries to answer it itself. If a tool already does that thing, it shows you the button and opens it. No ask is filed.
- If nothing does it, the box drafts a one-line description of what it *would* do. You edit the wording until it's right and press propose. Your words are the contract.
- The ask is saved with a timestamp, your text, and which tool you were in when you asked. It syncs to the server and to your other devices. Works offline — it sends itself when you're back.
- The monitor on my side sees it land and wakes me, usually within a second.
- I sort it: is it a duplicate, a setting, a switch, a bug, a new feature, or a decision that's really yours? Only new features and bugs get built.
- I mark it "being built". That shows up on your phone straight away, so you know it was picked up.
- I build it as a proper feature node. The ask itself is the provenance — your approved sentence becomes the feature's description, word for word.
- I ship it and mark it "shipped" with the build number. It leaves your requests list and appears in your awaiting-update list.
- You press update once, and all your devices take it.

The rule underneath: I never come back and ask you about it. You asked for a thing and you should get the thing.

**2) How that runs inside Claude Code**

- **Monitor tool** — the intake. It runs `tools/ask_monitor.py` in the background and pokes me when an ask arrives, even mid-conversation.
- **Bash** — the hands. ssh to the mini, `stamp_ask.py` to change the status on your phone, the linker, the deploy script.
- **Agent tool** — extra builders. If two asks land at once I can hand one to a subagent working in its own copy of the repo, so they don't tread on each other. Merging and deploying stay with me, one at a time.
- **Memory files** — the standing rules that survive between sessions, like the two you gave me today.
- **The transcript export** — turns our conversation into the citable record features point back to.

So the loop is: your phone writes to your world → the monitor wakes me → I build → deploy stamps it → your phone hears about it. The only human decision left in the middle is yours, at the start.

### p8
*2026-08-23 10:12*

> thanks, that's great. so I had a conversation with my friend Tom about this idea, and he came back with a couple of challenges, in particular one relating to the "don't ask". It seems like (in the situation that the app is connected to claude so we have full fable power available) the "draft" process (which currently just takes the user's initial request) could be improved to try and better understand the context within which the user is making the request. As developers for real users, we've long understood that when the user asks for a feature, they're often making the leap from "perceived problem" to "solution" themselves, but once the developer properly understands the problem, they would propose a better solution (given their knowledge of the code, and of other users). So there's a "context-understanding" dialogue that can drastically improve the proposal. I'd like to think this through with you and propose a better workflow.

Tom's challenge is a good one, and I think it's mostly right — but it lands on a narrower target than it looks.

**The rule isn't "don't talk to the user". It's "don't interrupt them later."**

Your original words were: never come back and ask me *here*. The problem being solved was a broken promise — someone files a wish, walks away expecting a feature, and instead gets a question in a channel they aren't watching.

A conversation at the moment of asking is the opposite of that. The user is standing right there, holding the phone, already thinking about the thing. That's the cheapest their attention will ever be.

And we already do a weak version of it. The propose box drafts a sentence and asks you to edit it. That *is* a dialogue — it's just a stupid one, because the drafter is a text template with no idea what you're doing.

So this isn't a new rule. It's the existing seam getting a brain.

**What the model would need to know**

Tom's point is that a developer proposes better solutions because they know the code and the other users. We can hand over most of that:

- The whole feature tree — every feature, what it does, in plain words. Already exported.
- Where you were standing when you asked. Already captured.
- **What you were doing in the last minute.** The blackbox records every tap. If you pressed reset five times before asking, the real problem is visible in the record, not in your sentence. I think this is the strongest signal and we currently throw it away.
- Your own past asks — what you've wanted before, what shipped.
- Other people's open asks — so two people wanting the same thing gets noticed at the moment of asking, not weeks later.

That's a lot of what a developer knows, available before the first word of reply.

**The workflow I'd propose**

1. You type a wish. Local search runs first, as now — instant, works offline, costs nothing. If a tool already does it, you get the button and we're done.
2. If not, the ask goes out with the context above.
3. It comes back with three things at once:
   - a proposed description, same as today;
   - **at most two questions** — and only where your answer would change what gets built;
   - or, sometimes, an answer instead: "that already exists, here", or "that's just a setting, I've changed it for you."
4. You can ignore all of it and press propose. That's today's behaviour, still one tap.
5. Whatever you settle on is the contract — unchanged.
6. The **whole exchange** gets filed, not just the final sentence. So the feature's record says what problem you had, not only what you asked for.

Offline, step 3 doesn't happen and the dumb template drafts as it does now. The flow must never depend on the network.

**Two things I'd hold firm on**

*Questions must be cheap.* Two maximum, offered as taps ("did you mean A or B?") rather than open prompts. Anything more is an interrogation, and people stop asking.

*A better idea is offered, never substituted.* Your law above the laws exists because I once shipped a position readout instead of a map. The fix isn't "propose worse things" — it's that if the model thinks there's a better solution, it puts it in front of you as a choice and you pick. Silently building something else is still forbidden. The difference is you're present to say yes.

**Three decisions I think are yours, not mine**

1. **The ask leaves the device.** This would be miso's first dependency on an outside service. For the campaign app — a trust-ring tool where people post things they don't want travelling — that's a real question, not a default. Does the wish text go out? Does the blackbox context go with it? For everyone, or only for you?
2. **Who pays, and what happens when it's not available.** Falling back to the template is honest but noticeably worse. Is that fine?
3. **Does a resolved conversation count as done?** If the answer is "that's a setting, changed it", nothing is built and nothing ships. I'd stamp it *answered* rather than *shipped* — but that's a new lifecycle state and it's your call.

There's also a fourth moment we don't use at all: after it ships. Your awaiting-update list already shows you what was built. "Is this what you meant?" is one tap away, and a no could reopen the conversation instead of becoming a new ask from scratch.

This is a design conversation, so no node yet. Tell me where you disagree and I'll write the settled version into `notes.md`.

### p9
*2026-08-23 10:18*

> yeah, that's a strong start. So the vision I had for miso (wider context) goes like this: the user is trying to achieve some goal / task (eg. "book a trip to China") and maybe some sub-task ("find a hotel in Shanghai"), in aid of which they are using tools eg. search / calendar / etc. Over time, we should be able to read the trace history of their tool use to a) extract some hypothesis about the task-tree [i.e. figure out they're trying to book a hotel in Shanghai / trip to China] or b) actually let them represent those tasks as first-class objects. Then, given the accumulated tool-use history, we can actually create new "emergent tools" such as "book a hotel in [city]" or "book a trip to [country]" that, by and large, do what the user would have done.

That's a much bigger machine, and the interesting thing is how much of it miso already has lying around.

**You've already built the trace.** The blackbox records every event, always, on the device, and ships it. Replay can re-drive a recorded session through the same update chains. Drive can tap buttons on command. So "read the history of tool use" and "do what the user would have done" both have working substrates already — they were built on day two for debugging, and they turn out to be the raw material for this.

That's the good news. Here's how I'd break the rest apart.

**Ask and trace are the same machine from two ends**

An ask is the user *telling* you the task. A trace is the user *showing* you it.

So the context pack I proposed an hour ago — "what were you doing in the last minute" — is just the first rung of this ladder. Build that and the ask conversation gets better immediately, before any of the ambitious parts exist. That's where I'd start, because it pays on day one.

**Infer, then offer. Never make them file paperwork.**

You named two options: infer the task tree, or let people represent tasks as first-class objects. I'd do both, in that order, joined by one move: **a task becomes an object when the user confirms a guess.**

Nobody creates task objects by hand. But almost everyone will tap "yes" on "looks like you're booking a trip to China?". Same shape as the ask dialogue — the system proposes, the person confirms, and the confirmation is what makes it real.

**The second occurrence is what reveals the variable**

This is the bit I like most, because it's a rule you already have.

Your promotion rule says a constant earns a variable when a second ask touches it. The same rule works here. One trace of booking a hotel in Shanghai is just a recording — you can't tell which parts are the point and which are incidental. A *second* trace, for Osaka, tells you exactly where the hole goes: the parts that differ are the parameters, the parts that stayed are the tool.

So "book a hotel in [city]" is not a clever generalisation problem. It's a diff between two traces. That's cheap and it's checkable.

**An emergent tool should be a real feature node**

This is what would make it miso rather than a macro recorder. The synthesized tool gets written as a node, with a description, a toggle, and provenance — and the provenance is *the traces it came from*. That's a third kind of citation alongside conversations and asks: the thing you did five times.

It then rides the machinery that already exists: it shows up in your awaiting list, you approve it once, it reaches all your devices, you can untick it if it's wrong.

**A rough ladder**

1. Traces the server can read back per user. Mostly exists.
2. Cut the stream into episodes — tool opened, tool closed, long pause. No model needed.
3. Name an episode. Model reads it, guesses, offers you the guess. Yes / no / fix the wording.
4. Group episodes into goals over days. Only worth doing once naming works.
5. Spot episodes that rhyme. Exact rhymes need no model at all.
6. On the second rhyme, offer the tool, with the diff as its parameters.
7. Ship it as a node.

Rungs 1–2 improve the ask box. Rung 3 is the first thing a user would notice. Rungs 5–6 are the payoff.

**Three things I'd flag honestly**

*The current tools are toys.* Taps and dictate don't generate traces worth mining. The mechanism can still be proven on them — the same way the compute substrate proved itself on a multiply kernel it didn't need — but the real value waits for tools that do things with consequences.

*Doing what the user would have done is safe for looking and dangerous for acting.* Searching, filtering, reading — fine to replay. Booking, paying, messaging someone — the tool should get to the last step and stop. That boundary needs to be in the design from birth, not added after the first bad surprise.

*Traces are more private than asks.* An ask is a sentence you chose to write. A trace is everywhere you went. If any of this leaves the device, that's a much heavier decision than the one we were just discussing — and for the campaign app it may be a no.

**A cheap experiment we could run now**

We have real blackbox logs on the mini. Before designing anything, take a day of your actual recorded sessions and see whether a model can say what you were doing, from the events alone. If it can't name a task from a real trace, rungs 3–6 don't exist yet and we'd know that for the cost of an afternoon.

Want me to write this up in `notes.md` as the design record, and run that experiment?
